messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

### Clinical Vignette: Mr. Hassan Mr. Hassan is a 54-year-old Middle Eastern man who has been married for over three decades and works as a community organizer in his local neighborhood. His recent struggle with PTSD emerged after experiencing physical abuse from his romantic partner, an event that continues to haunt him. The traumatic incident occurred at night when he was home alone. The darkness of the room amplified the fear and vulnerability he felt during the assault. Since then, dark spaces have become a potent trigger for Mr. Hassan. He avoids entering basements or dimly lit areas, as these settings instantly bring back fragments of the terrifying event. These memories are often accompanied by auditory triggers, such as sounds resembling aircraft helicopters, which remind him of the night he was attacked. Mr. Hassan has developed several maladaptive strategies to cope with his trauma. He is hypervigilant around people and avoids going near the location where the assault took place. Additionally, he wears concealing clothing to avoid drawing attention to himself, a behavior that stemmed from his belief that he could have prevented the abuse if he had been more inconspicuous. The event has fragmented his memories into disconnected pieces, making it difficult for him to form a coherent narrative of what happened. These fragments resurface without warning, often triggered by something in his surroundings. The auditory recall is particularly distressing; whenever he hears aircraft sounds, the memory of that night becomes vivid and overpowering, causing intense anxiety. Mr. Hassan has come to believe that the abuse was inevitable due to a fundamental flaw within himself—the kind of person he is—and this belief has shattered his trust in others. He feels betrayed by someone he trusted deeply and now questions many of his core beliefs about how the world works. These negative appraisals have reinforced his hypervigilance, as he believes that being constantly on guard will prevent similar incidents from happening again. The memories and their fragmented nature exacerbate his maladaptive strategies. He avoids dark spaces to prevent reliving those terrifying moments and stays vigilant around people, fearing that another betrayal could occur at any time. These behaviors have led to significant changes in his daily life. His work as a community organizer has been impacted because he often finds himself unable to attend meetings held in dimly lit community centers or events where helicopters are present. The cycle of hypervigilance and avoidance has become self-reinforcing, leading to increased anxiety and a sense that the world is an inherently dangerous place. His maladaptive strategies have not only reinforced his negative appraisals but also created new triggers. For example, wearing concealing clothing to avoid attention has made him more aware of people's gazes, heightening his hypervigilance. Mr. Hassan’s relationship with his spouse has also been strained as a result of these changes in behavior. He often feels misunderstood and isolated, believing that no one can truly understand what he is going through. These feelings have led to increased tension and a sense of emotional distance between them. Ultimately, it was the impact on his work and relationships that prompted Mr. Hassan to seek help. The most pressing fear for him is the possibility of another betrayal or attack, while his greatest hope lies in finding a way to regain trust and rebuild his shattered beliefs about the world. He is looking for a sense of safety and security, hoping to break free from the cycle of hypervigilance and avoidance that has dominated his life since the traumatic event. Mr. Hassan’s narrative illustrates the complex interplay between triggers, maladaptive strategies, fragmented memories, and negative appraisals. Each component reinforces the others, creating a tight loop that has made it increasingly difficult for him to navigate everyday life without feeling overwhelmed by fear and anxiety.
